title: Finding the Atom's Parts
objective: After this level you can explain Thomson's and Rutherford's experiments.
summary: Thomson found the electron in 1897 and pictured a plum pudding atom. In 1909 alpha particles bounced back off gold foil, and in 1911 Rutherford explained it with a tiny, dense nucleus.

cards.headline: The day a shell bounced off tissue paper (almost)
cards.body: That is roughly how Ernest Rutherford described one result from his lab. To see why it stunned him, start with the atom everyone believed in before.

cards.headline: Thomson finds the electron
cards.body: In 1897, J.J. Thomson was studying cathode rays, made by driving electricity through a tube with most of the air pumped out. He concluded they were particles far lighter than any atom, and that all matter contains them. He called them corpuscles; we call them electrons. The uncuttable atom had a piece you could knock off.

cards.headline: The plum pudding
cards.body: Atoms carry no overall charge, so something positive had to balance those negative electrons. Thomson pictured a sphere of evenly spread positive matter with electrons stuck in it, like plums in a pudding. Positive charge everywhere, spread thin.
cards.callout: Plum pudding: spread-out positive, with electrons as the plums

cards.headline: The gold foil surprise
cards.body: In 1909, Hans Geiger and Ernest Marsden, working with Rutherford, fired alpha particles at thin gold foil. Most went straight through. A very few bounced almost straight back, which the plum pudding couldn't explain. Rutherford said it was "almost as incredible as if you fired a 15-inch shell at a piece of tissue paper and it came back and hit you."

cards.headline: A tiny, heavy heart
cards.body: In 1911 Rutherford explained it: an atom's positive charge and nearly all its mass sit in a tiny nucleus, with electrons around it and mostly empty space between. Most alpha particles miss the nucleus entirely; the rare near-hits bounce back. In 1932, James Chadwick found the last piece: the neutron.

cards.headline: Atom's parts: found
learned: His plum pudding: electrons in spread-out positive matter
Gold foil, 1909: most passed through, a few bounced back
Rutherford, 1911: a tiny, dense nucleus; Chadwick, 1932: the neutron

questions.prompt: By studying cathode rays in 1897, J.J. Thomson discovered _____.
questions.explanation: Thomson showed cathode rays are particles far lighter than atoms, found in all matter: electrons.

questions.prompt: Match each scientist with what the level credits to them.
questions.explanation: Thomson pictured the plum pudding atom, Rutherford put the positive charge in a tiny nucleus, and James Chadwick found the neutron.

questions.prompt: Level 13 called the atom mostly empty space. Which gold foil result pointed to that?

options.label: A very few alpha particles bounced back
options.rationale: That pointed to the tiny, dense nucleus.

options.label: The foil glowed with the plum pudding's light
The foil turned into lead
options.rationale: The foil wasn't changed into anything.

options.label: Most alpha particles went straight through

questions.explanation: If most particles sail straight through, most of each atom must be empty space.
